about: Family sheets: the family ID marks, behaviour, habitat and size lines and the extra "don't confuse with" lines (Pierre's answers of 2026-11-06 to the fish-sheets study, Q7, Q11; 16:54: published on the sheets at once, he corrects them in place). Our own words, written from the sources each family lists (src) and faithful to the IMR fish presentation, whose cues the sheet shows apart. marks: what identifies the family, beyond IMR's cues; life: behaviour, habitat, size; apart: {family id: a line telling it from that family}, only for pairs IMR gives no words for. Built into fish.json families (tools/build_fish.py add_families: marks, life, apart, msrc).

marks: Deep, flattened body with a small mouth
Colours vary between individuals and between places for the same species
life: Many are territorial; they eat algae, small animals or plankton
Males guard the eggs, laid on the bottom
Anemonefishes (Amphiprion) live with large sea anemones
Most are small, at most about 35 cm

marks: Very flat, deep body; small mouth at the tip of the snout, with brush-like teeth
Scales run onto the dorsal and anal fins
Many have a dark band through the eye and an eyespot towards the back
life: Most live in male-female pairs, active by day near coral reefs
Many eat coral polyps, small invertebrates and algae; some eat plankton

marks: The gill-cover spine sits at the corner of its front bone (the preopercle), on the cheek
Many have a trailing tip at the back of the dorsal and anal fins
Tail rounded to deeply crescent-shaped
life: Mostly shallower than 20 m, rarely below 50 m, near coral reefs
Pairs or harems; many change sex from female to male
Centropyge eat mostly algae, Genicanthus plankton, most others sponges and invertebrates

marks: Deep body, very flat from the side, with a small mouth
life: Eat algae and small invertebrates

marks: Disc-shaped, very flat body; long tube-like snout with a small mouth
Dorsal spines drawn out into a long whip-like filament
No spine on the tail base, unlike the surgeonfishes
life: Common on coral reefs; eats mainly sponges and other bottom invertebrates

apart.f:Surgeonfishes: Surgeonfish: a spine on the tail base, no long dorsal filament

marks: Eye set high on the head, well back from the small mouth
One long dorsal fin without a notch
Very small scales
life: Most graze algae on the bottom; some eat plankton or detritus
Can slash other fish with the tail spine by a quick sweep of the tail

apart.f:MoorishIdol: Moorish Idol: no spine on the tail base, long whip-like dorsal filament
apart.f:Rabbitfishes: Rabbitfish: no spine on the tail base, a spine at each end of the pelvic fins

marks: Each pelvic fin has a spine at both ends, with 3 soft rays between
13 strong dorsal spines, venomous
life: Active by day, eating algae on the bottom
Some swim in schools, others stay among corals; up to about 40 cm

apart.f:Surgeonfishes: Surgeonfish: a spine on the tail base, eye high on the head

marks: Teeth fused into a beak
Large scales
life: Scrape algae off dead coral; the rock they swallow comes out as sand, so they make much of the reef's sand
Some sleep at night inside a mucus cocoon
Initial phase (females and males) and brightly coloured terminal males look different

marks: Mouth can be pushed forward
life: Most change colour and sex as they grow: an initial phase, then terminal males
Most eat bottom invertebrates; some eat plankton; small cleaner wrasses pick parasites off larger fish
Many bury themselves in the sand
Most are under 15 cm; the largest reach 2.3 m

marks: Large canine teeth in the jaws
Dorsal fin continuous or slightly notched
Upper jaw slides under the cheek bone when the mouth is closed
life: Most hunt crustaceans and fish near the bottom; some eat plankton
Up to about 1 m

apart.f:Fusiliers: Fusilier: small mouth, deeply forked tail, in large schools

marks: Dorsal fin with 10 spines and 9-10 soft rays
life: Feed on the bottom on invertebrates and fish, mostly at night
Alone or in schools, not territorial

marks: Some species have a filament off the upper lobe of the tail
life: Eat small bottom fish, squid and octopus, crustaceans and worms; some eat plankton

marks: Gill cover with three flat spines: a main one with one above and one below
Tail usually rounded, square or crescent-shaped, rarely forked
End of the upper jaw still visible with the mouth closed
life: Bottom-dwelling predators; up to 3 m
Start as females and change into males

marks: Soapfishes get their name from a bitter skin toxin (grammistin)
life: Eat crustaceans and fish

marks: Small mouth with thick lips
Enlarged pores under the chin
life: Active at night: by day they shelter under ledges, often in groups, and disperse at dusk to feed on bottom invertebrates
Up to about 60 cm

marks: Small and colourful
life: Eat plankton, mostly tiny crustaceans and fish eggs
Females change into a few dominant males

marks: Small mouth that can be pushed far forward
Black spot at the base of the pectoral fin
Scale rows run along the body
life: Up to about 50 cm

apart.f:Snappers: Snapper: larger mouth with canine teeth, tail only shallowly notched

marks: No spiny dorsal fin: one small soft dorsal fin
Mouth cannot be pushed forward
life: Eat small invertebrates attached to the bottom, and algae
Territorial; a male with several females
Up to about 60 cm

apart.f:Puffers: Puffer: no bony box; can inflate itself

marks: Two dorsal fins far apart
Many are brightly coloured
life: Probe sand and holes in the reef with their barbels for invertebrates and small fish
Up to about 60 cm

marks: Very thick, tough skin with large, plate-like scales
Strong teeth; small gill slit in front of the pectoral fin
life: Swim by waving the second dorsal and anal fins; the tail for bursts of speed
Mostly alone and active by day; eat invertebrates, including hard-shelled molluscs and echinoderms
Usually from just below the surface to 50 m on coral reefs

marks: Four fused teeth, two above and two below, like a beak
Skin naked or with small prickles on the belly
life: Lay eggs in a nest on the bottom
Sharpnose puffers (Canthigaster) are the small ones of the family

apart.f:Boxfishes: Boxfish: body in a rigid bony box

marks: The second dorsal spine is much smaller than the first
Teeth made for nibbling
life: Eat bottom invertebrates; some eat coral or plankton
Eggs laid in a spot the male, or both parents, guard

marks: Head with ridges and spines
Venom glands in the dorsal, anal and pelvic spines
life: Live on or near the bottom; eat crustaceans and fish

marks: Large, very rough scales; spiny edge to the gill cover
Forked tail
life: Hide by day in crevices or under ledges; out at night
Eat large plankton
Most on coral or rocky reefs; some in seagrass or on soft bottoms; from near shore to about 300 m

marks: Large, very rough scales; spiny edge to the gill cover
Forked tail
life: Hide by day in crevices or under ledges; out at night
Eat bottom invertebrates and small fish

marks: Cylindrical body; fins without spines
Large mouth full of slender, sharp teeth, even on the tongue
life: Voracious predators of small fish

marks: Pelvic fins set under or in front of the pectoral fins
Dorsal fin with 4-5 spines and a long soft part
life: Eat small bottom invertebrates and fish
Territorial; a male with several females
